diseases.summary: Rust pustules spread quickly in humid conditions and can weaken photosynthesis if ignored.
symptoms: Small cinnamon-brown raised pustules on both leaf surfaces.
Scattered spots become denser as humidity stays high.
Older leaves are usually affected first.
management: Monitor disease pressure across several plants before spraying.
Use resistant seed varieties where available next season.
Consult local extension guidance if disease reaches upper leaves early.
prevention: Avoid continuous maize cropping in the same plot.
Promote field airflow with correct spacing.
nextSteps: Rescan 2 more leaves from different plants.
Record whether lesions are moving toward the upper canopy.
Compare with the disease library before treatment.
diseases.rescanAdvice: Capture a bright close-up from the middle of the leaf where pustules are visible.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate if rust reaches the top leaves before tasseling or spreads fast after rain.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: Brown raised spots mean you should check more plants before spraying.

diseases.summary: Gray leaf spot forms narrow rectangular lesions that can merge and dry leaves prematurely.
symptoms: Long rectangular gray or tan lesions following leaf veins.
Lesions may join together and cause blighting.
Disease is more intense in warm, humid fields.
management: Prioritize early scouting when humidity remains high.
Use residue and rotation management to reduce inoculum.
Seek expert advice if upper canopy infection is visible before grain fill.
prevention: Choose tolerant varieties in hotspot areas.
nextSteps: Inspect the lower and middle canopy for similar rectangular lesions.
Note moisture conditions in the field journal.
Repeat scanning after 3-5 days if symptoms are spreading.
diseases.rescanAdvice: Frame one clear lesion band and avoid shadows across the leaf.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate if lesions are numerous in the upper canopy or leaves are drying rapidly.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: Long gray blocks on the leaf can mean strong disease pressure.

diseases.summary: The sampled leaf does not show strong signs of the trained disease classes.
symptoms: No strong lesion pattern is visible.
No major disease cues detected by the model.
management: Check other plants if the field still looks stressed.
Keep irrigation and nutrition records up to date.
prevention: Keep field hygiene and weed control strong.
Watch for sudden changes after wet weather.
nextSteps: Scan another plant if nearby leaves look different.
Use the field journal to record healthy checkpoints.
Return to the dashboard for trend tracking.
diseases.rescanAdvice: If the field still looks stressed, scan a leaf with the clearest visible symptoms.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate only if many plants show stress that the app cannot classify clearly.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: This leaf looks okay, but still check other plants in the field.

diseases.summary: This is a high-risk disease complex that can severely reduce yield and needs urgent field attention.
symptoms: Chlorotic mottling and necrotic streaking on leaves.
Plants may become stunted or fail to fill grain.
management: Isolate heavily affected plants where practical.
Control insect vectors and remove volunteer maize.
Contact extension support urgently for field-wide advice.
prevention: Use clean seed and certified sources.
Reduce vector pressure early in the season.
Destroy volunteer hosts around the field.
nextSteps: Scan more plants around the affected patch.
Mark the field area in the journal.
diseases.rescanAdvice: Capture a full leaf with visible streaking and one closer image of the lesion pattern.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate immediately when several plants show similar symptoms in one area.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: If many leaves show yellow and dead streaks, ask an expert quickly.

diseases.summary: Fine chlorotic streaks can signal viral infection spread by leafhoppers, especially in young plants.
symptoms: Fine yellow streaks running along the leaf.
Stunting is more serious in young maize.
Symptoms may appear uneven across the field.
management: Rogue badly infected plants where feasible.
Reduce vector pressure and alternate hosts.
Check planting timing and nearby grassy weeds.
prevention: Control grassy hosts around the field.
nextSteps: Compare symptoms across young and older plants.
Record any leafhopper pressure in notes.
Rescan after improving image clarity if streaks are faint.
diseases.rescanAdvice: Use bright natural light and keep the streaks centered in the frame.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate if young plants are heavily stunted or symptoms are spreading quickly.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: Thin yellow lines on many young leaves can mean virus risk.

diseases.summary: Large cigar-shaped lesions can expand fast and reduce grain filling when disease pressure is high.
symptoms: Lesions may enlarge and merge under wet conditions.
Disease often starts on lower leaves before moving upward.
management: Track whether lesions are moving to the upper canopy.
Use resistant varieties in future seasons.
Seek agronomy advice if pressure is high before tasseling.
prevention: Avoid susceptible varieties in hotspot regions.
nextSteps: Scan multiple leaves from different plants.
Document lesion size and spread in the journal.
Review prevention steps in the disease library.
diseases.rescanAdvice: Take one image showing the full lesion shape and one closer image with clear edges.
diseases.escalateWhen: Escalate if lesions are large, numerous, and already reaching the upper canopy.
diseases.lowLiteracyTip: Big cigar-shaped marks can mean a serious blight problem.
